Career Area:

Technology, Digital and Data

Job Description:

Your Work Shapes the World at Caterpillar Inc.

When you join Caterpillar, you're joining a global team who cares not just about the work we do – but also about each other. We are the makers, problem solvers, and future world builders who are creating stronger, more sustainable communities. We don't just talk about progress and innovation here – we make it happen, with our customers, where we work and live. Together, we are building a better world, so we can all enjoy living in it.

Job Summary:

As an Autonomy Systems Engineer, on the Surface Loading Autonomy team you will be an integral part of the team developing the next generation of autonomous machines for the construction industry. In this role you will have responsibility to help to define the requirements and system architecture to integrate autonomy solutions with the base machine, integrating many different types of onboard electronics system, and includes hands on work in both lab and on machine environments. The incumbent needs to be very detail oriented, help to develop and execute standard work and work well with and through others. Additionally, the incumbent will also need to be capable of making and communicating good decisions around the trade-offs between time, resources, and quality.

What You Will Do:

  • Apply new autonomous system solutions and technologies on a semi or full autonomous system
  • Decomposition of Customer requirements into (L6) system level requirements
  • Work closely with Machine System teams (L6) to determine the best way to deliver on machine autonomous features.
  • Ensure clear documentation and traceability.
  • Integration and validation of autonomy solutions on surface loading machines
  • Serve as a subject matter expert for Surface Loading Machine Autonomous Solutions
  • Communicate system readiness and technical risk to stakeholders

What You Will Have:

Communicating Complex Concepts:

  • Work with a global team to communicate the Why’s and develop the How’s of agreed features.
  • Clearly document the details for the system and ensure understanding and compliance with each subsystem team.
  • Communicate designs and tradeoffs with stakeholders at multiple levels.

Technical Excellence:

  • Proven ability to work on production products through design, implementation, customer rollout, and support.
  • Ability to decompose complex customer requirements into achievable technical requirements for the systems that make up the product.
  • Knowledge and experience with autonomous systems and hardware, including vision systems (e.g. Camera, Lidar, and Radar), G&SS, and IMU.

Influencing Through Expertise:

  • Strong working knowledge of the Autonomy ecosystem in mining or construction, or other autonomous system control system architectures which can be drawn upon for design proposals and decisions.
  • Constantly staying abreast of advancements in the Autonomy and construction industries.
  • Provides evidentiary support while giving opinions or recommendations to influence decision making.
  • Conducts tasks in such a way as to build a strong reputation and credibility as an expert in the field.

Effective Communications:

  • Effectively communicates ideas and design tradeoffs to team members and stakeholders
  • Willing to spend the time to document designs, requirements, and success criteria to ensure team member alignment
  • Clearly explains project goals to team members, keeps leadership informed of progress, and shares relevant updates with external partners
  • Uses data-driven arguments, active listening, and tailored messaging to persuade stakeholders and achieve consensus.

W. There are several ways to define research and to provide details about its specific methodology. A search of the literature will provide some examples. Here, the meaning of research as a process is described, with an emphasis on research as a process that produces a reliable (valid, consistent) and useful result. This is a crucial distinction. What do these words mean in general? A reliable result is not simply a correct answer to a question (although a correct answer is always a good thing). A reliable result is an answer that is based on observations that are consistently produced under specific conditions. Reliability in this sense refers to the dependability or consistency of a test or measurement, whether a method or a process. Reliability is a necessary condition for a result to be considered valid; that is, for a result to be considered true. The concept of reliability is fundamental to the scientific method. Without it, the results of any scientific investigation are not to be trusted. In other words, a study must be repeatable. The same method, under the same conditions, should produce the same results. This is the essence of reproducibility. Reproducibility is the ability to recreate a prior finding or set of findings. It is a critical component of scientific rigor and integrity. This concept is discussed in more detail later in this guide. The concept of validity is also fundamental. It refers to the degree to which a test, instrument, or process actually measures what it purports to measure. If a test is not valid, it does not measure what it is supposed to measure. In other words, it is not an accurate or true measure of what it claims to measure. Validity is a more complex concept than reliability. There are different types of validity: internal validity, external validity, construct validity, and content validity. Internal validity refers to the extent to which a study establishes a cause-and-effect relationship between the independent and dependent variables. External validity refers to the extent to which the results of a study can be generalized to other populations, settings, and times. Construct validity refers to the extent to which a test measures the theoretical construct or attribute it is intended to measure. Content validity refers to the extent to which a test measures all aspects of the construct it is intended to measure. These concepts are important in research, as they help to ensure that the results of the research are trustworthy and meaningful. These concepts are discussed in more detail later in this guide.
